newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN Burundi forum postponed as Swiss deny visas.
newsitem.headline: UN Burundi forum postponed as Swiss deny visas.

text.p: A U.N. forum for dialogue in Burundi was postponed on Monday after the Swiss government denied visas to some of the Burundian participants, diplomats said.

Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Yasmine Chatila declined to say on what grounds the visas were denied. "We can confirm that visas have been denied. We had problems giving visas to some of the Burundians," she told Reuters.

Diplomats said the decision affected four participants to the forum for Burundian politicians, religious leaders and civil representatives, organised by UNESCO, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation.

They said the four included members of a parliamentary delegation from Uprona party, dominated by minority Tutsis and an opponent of a government strategy of negotiating with the main Hutu rebel group, the exiled National Council for the Defence of Democracy.
Chatila said UNESCO decided to postpone the forum before the Swiss government officially informed it of its decision on visas. She gave no details.
UNESCO officials earlier said the meeting was postponed to a future date because of difficulties in getting all the participants to Geneva but did not elaborate.

Diplomats said the Swiss decision was just one of the problems. Burundians were not able to agree until the last minute on a final list of participants, adding to the delay. "Everyone is very embarrassed," said one diplomat.

The Geneva forum was intended to complement peace moves in the small landlocked central African country to end a vicious civil war between the almost exclusively Tutsi army, which took power in a coup last July, and Hutu rebels.
After the coup by army major Pierre Buyoya, which toppled the civilian Hutu president, leaders of Burundi's predominantly Hutu FRODEBU Party fled to exile.
A majority of members of the parliament elected in 1993 are in exile or were killed during nearly four years of violence that have cost more than 150,000 lives in a population of just six million.
The United Nations human rights office in Geneva says the army has killed thousands of civilians so far this year.
African countries slapped regional sanctions on Burundi after the coup, demanding restoration of civilian rule and direct negotiations between the two sides.
